extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of history of mathematics and classical Greek geometry
extracted.subtask_description: A chapter-level historical survey summarizing what portions of Euclid's Elements and related mathematical knowledge (proof methods, classifications of irrationals, constructions) were known or developed up to Plato's time, and the methods used to establish key theorems (e.g., incommensurability, method of exhaustion, duplication of the cube).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of Pythagorean geometry relative to Euclid
rubrics_metrics.description: The Pythagorean geometry already contained the substance of Euclid's Books I and II, part of Book IV, and theorems corresponding to a great part of Book VI; by Hippocrates' time the main propositions of Book III were known and used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is used as a criterion for judging which parts of Euclid's Elements had essentially existed in earlier Pythagorean mathematics: plane geometry (I-II) and many proportionality/number results (VII-VIII) were largely in place, whereas Euclid's Book V (Eudoxean theory of proportion) was not. Example: Hippocrates assumes theorems Eucl. III.20-22 and constructions like Eucl. III.33; Book III geometry (circle segments, angles in semicircles) is attributed to that period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of exhaustion and dependence on Archimedes' Axiom
rubrics_metrics.description: Euclid proves XII.2 (circles are to one another as the squares on their diameters) by the method of exhaustion, the invention of which is attributed to Eudoxus; this method depends on a lemma known as the Axiom of Archimedes (or an equivalent lemma, e.g. Eucl. X.1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rigorous area/volume ratio proofs (method of exhaustion) require an underpinning lemma (Archimedes's Axiom/Eucl. X.1). The text notes that if Hippocrates gave an earlier genuine proof of XII.2, it would imply some anticipation 'in essence' of the method of exhaustion. Thus, when assessing claims of an ancient proof by exhaustion, check for an explicit use or anticipation of the Archimedean lemma.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessary constructive proof for existence of incommensurable ratios (porism to Eucl. X.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove the existence of incommensurable ratios it was necessary to give a geometrical construction: given a straight line a and numbers m,n one must find a straight line x such that a:x = m:n, and then take y a mean proportional between a and x to construct an irrational straight line a √(n/m).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text treats the porism to Eucl. X.6 as the standard method to demonstrate existence of irrational straight lines: existence must be shown by explicit construction, not merely asserted. Use this constructive approach when claiming the existence of particular irrationals in classical geometry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three candidate methods for proving incommensurability (Theodorus' cases)
rubrics_metrics.description: Theodorus's proofs that √3, √5, ... up to √17 are incommensurable may have used one of: (1) successive rational approximations (Hultsch hypothesis), (2) an adaptation of the classical reductio ad absurdum used for √2 (parity/divisibility argument), or (3) the Euclidean process of finding the greatest common measure (Zeuthen hypothesis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text evaluates these methods: (1) successive approximations may suggest irrationality but cannot prove incommensurability; (2) adapting the √2 parity proof to other primes (3,5,...) is straightforward but would be an obvious routine adaptation (hence possibly too trivial to be historically noteworthy); (3) Zeuthen's hypothesis uses the algorithmic subtraction/G.C.M. process (Eucl. X.2) and can yield a convincing geometric demonstration by showing the process never terminates (recurrence), illustrated by detailed constructions for √5, √3 and √2. When reconstructing ancient proofs, prefer (3) if one seeks an explanation that both justifies Plato's remark and requires separate casework up to √17.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation of successive approximation method
rubrics_metrics.description: The method of finding successive rational approximations (e.g., continued fraction–like trials) might produce closer and closer fractions approximating a surd but would not constitute a proof of incommensurability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat such approximation methods as heuristic only. The text explicitly rejects them as sufficient proofs of incommensurability: they can suggest irrationality but do not demonstrate impossibility of exact rational expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reductio (parity/divisibility) adaptation for other surds
rubrics_metrics.description: The traditional reductio ad absurdum proof used for √2 can be adapted for √3, √5, etc., by substituting divisibility by the corresponding integer; this yields a contradiction that the numerator and denominator are both divisible by that integer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although straightforward and valid, the text suggests this adaptation is so direct that it would be unnecessary to repeat it case by case up to √17, and therefore may not explain why Theodorus's lecture singled out those cases. Use of this proof is acceptable as a rigorous method but historically might be considered routine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Euclidean G.C.M. (subtraction) method for proving incommensurability
rubrics_metrics.description: If the process of finding the greatest common measure (continual subtraction of the lesser from the greater) never ends, the magnitudes are incommensurable (Eucl. X.2). Zeuthen hypothesizes Theodorus used this criterion, proceeding geometrically to show recurrence/never-terminating remainder sequences for particular surds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This method provides a convincing geometric demonstration of incommensurability by showing an infinite descent/recurrence. The text illustrates the method geometrically for √5 and √3 (cutting off equal segments and producing a diminishing infinite sequence of similar triangles). It also notes that the rigorous justification of Eucl. X.2 depends on X.1 (Archimedean-type lemma), which is later, but Theodorus might have used it intuitively or as a postulate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of rigorous arithmetical foundations (Books VII–VIII) for proofs in Book X
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs of certain propositions about irrationality (e.g., Eucl. X.9) formally depend on arithmetical propositions in Euclid's Books VII and VIII (e.g., VII.17–18, VII.27, VIII.2); a rigorous theory of numerical proportion and divisibility underpins the theory of irrationals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing the historical development of proofs about irrationals, check for the presence of the necessary number-theoretic propositions. The text presents Zeuthen's suggestion that Theaetetus may have innovated in Book VII material to support his theory of irrationals, but also offers reasons to doubt that all such arithmetic was absent from Pythagorean mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification and extension of irrationals (Theaetetus → Euclid)
rubrics_metrics.description: Theaetetus distinguished 'square roots' commensurable in length vs those only commensurable in square, and divided irrationals into genera (medial, binomial, apotome). Euclid later systematized and extended these distinctions into many orders (Eucl. X), proving there are thirteen irrational straight lines and showing how further irrationals derive from given ones (e.g., X.115).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical credit: Theaetetus laid the foundation and provided informal classification; Euclid provided rigorous definitions, distinctions between rational and irrational magnitudes, and an extended taxonomy. Use Theaetetus for origin of concepts and Euclid for formal/systematic criteria and exhaustive listings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive approach to the five regular solids (Theaetetus/Book XIII)
rubrics_metrics.description: Theaetetus is credited with 'constructing' or writing on the five regular solids (octahedron, icosahedron etc.), and his constructions formed the basis of Euclid's Book XIII which constructs the five regular solids, inscribes them in spheres, and relates their dimensions to circumscribing spheres.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognition of work on regular solids in the Elements requires explicit geometric constructions and relations to spheres; Theaetetus provided the ideas and constructions incorporated into Euclid. When evaluating claims about classical constructions, look for explicit construction steps and sphere-inscription relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Higher-geometry constructions required for duplication of the cube
rubrics_metrics.description: Archytas's solution of the problem of finding two mean proportionals (equivalent to duplication of the cube) used a remarkable three-dimensional construction and therefore belongs to higher geometry rather than plane Elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To account for classical solutions to cube-duplication, allow for three-dimensional constructions (solid geometry) beyond the plane techniques of early Elements. When reconstructing ancient solutions, consider spatial (3D) loci and methods, not just planar constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of analysis as a discovery technique
rubrics_metrics.description: Proclus' account (via Plato and Leodamas) attributes to Plato the method of inquiry by analysis: carrying the thing sought up to an acknowledged principle (working backwards from desired conclusion to known principles) as a fine method for discovering lemmas in geometry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a methodological criterion for discovering proofs/lemmas, analysis (working backward) should be recognized alongside synthetic presentation. Use analysis to find steps/lemmas to be later reversed into constructive/synthetic proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arithmetic propositions as prerequisites for certain geometric number-theory proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Archytas's proof that there can be no number which is a geometric mean between two superparticular numbers ((n+1):n) cites known propositions corresponding to Euclid Book VII (e.g., existence of least numbers in a ratio, properties of prime-to-one-another numbers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrations about number ratios or properties like non-existence of integer means rely on arithmetical propositions (divisibility, least numbers in a ratio). When evaluating ancient number-theoretic proofs embedded in geometry, ensure the underlying arithmetical lemmas are present or invoked.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summary criterion for what comprised the Elements by Plato's time
rubrics_metrics.description: By Plato's time: substance of Euclid Books I–IV was practically complete; Book V (Eudoxus' theory) was missing; numerical proportion theory (Book VII) probably existed in a Pythagorean form; much of Books VIII–IX, XI–XIII (including constructions for solids) and the foundation for Book X (irrationals) were in existence though possibly in different arrangement and methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this summary as a checklist for evaluating claims about the historical completeness of the Elements at a given date: check presence/absence of Eudoxean proportion, existence of arithmetic treatises akin to Euclid VII, and whether methods like exhaustion were in use. The text emphasizes that form and arrangement differed even where substance was present.
